bib.title: Exp3 for Adversarial Linear Bandits (Chapter 27 of Bandit Algorithms)
bib.venue: book chapter, Bandit Algorithms (Cambridge University Press)

question: How can exponential weights be adapted to adversarial linear bandits so that information is shared across actions and regret scales with dimension d rather than number of actions k?
contributions: Algorithm 15: exponential weights with least-squares loss estimates and Kiefer-Wolfowitz exploration mixing
Regret bound 2 sqrt(3 d n log k) for finite action sets
Continuous exponential weights for convex action sets with regret 2d sqrt(3n(1+log+(2n/d)))

limits: No experiments or numerical examples; all results are upper bounds on regret.
Algorithm 15 needs a finite A and costs O(kd+d^3) per round; k can be exponential in d.
Sampling algorithms for the continuous version are not very practical (authors' warning).
Kiefer-Wolfowitz exploration distribution must be computed; any pi with a bound on g(pi) suffices.
Assumes losses bounded in L and A spans R^d (relaxable by exercises).
practices: Estimate the loss vector by least squares, Yhat_t = Q_t^{-1} A_t Y_t with Q_t = sum_a P_t(a) a a^T, which is unbiased given history (Sec 27.1).
Mix exponential weights with an exploration distribution pi (Kiefer-Wolfowitz, g(pi)<=d) so Q_t is non-singular and estimates stay bounded (Sec 27.1, Thm 27.1).
Set gamma = eta g(pi) and eta = sqrt(log k / ((2g(pi)+d)n)) (p.321).
For large or infinite convex action sets use continuous exponential weights sampled via log-concave sampling (Sec 27.3).
For changing action sets with identities, choose a new exploration distribution each round (Note 4, Exercise 27.5).
Loss range b or [a,b]: rescale the algorithm (Exercises 27.2, 27.3).
